guide.orbitalis.accumulators.text:
The accumulator stores electricity, with nothing to set up. Its gauge faces you: energy comes in through every side but the back, and goes out through the back. Right-click to see its charge and how long until it is full or empty.

Four generations, each crafted around the previous one: 1, 4, 16 then 64 million FE. Upgrading keeps the energy already stored.

guide.orbitalis.arc_foundry.text:
The arc foundry melts two ingredients into an alloy. Place it against a generator and put the ingredients in the blue slots: the result comes out in the orange one.
- iron + coal = steel (10 s)
- 4 aluminum + 1 lithium = 5 aluminum-lithium (15 s)

"Not enough energy": refuel the generator. "Output full": empty the orange slot.

guide.orbitalis.conduits.text:
Conduits link machines at a distance. Placed end to end, they connect on their own.
- Energy cable: power, shared between the machines on the network.
- Fluid pipe: water, RP-1, liquid propellants.
- Gas pipe: hydrogen and oxygen gas.
- Data cable: links consoles, screens and data ports.

Give each liquid its own network if you fill several tanks.

A machine pushes what it makes, a tank does not. To empty one, sneak and right-click the pipe touching it with an empty hand: it starts pulling. Same gesture to switch back.

Right-click a pipe with an empty hand to change its color. Two pipes of different colors never connect, even side by side; a pipe with no color connects to all. Placed against a launch pad port, a pipe takes its propellant's color, and a pipe placed on a colored pipe carries its color on.

guide.orbitalis.crewed_flight.text:
The crew capsule ("Crew Capsules" technology) goes under the launch escape tower. With the rocket on the table, right-click the cabin to board; the first one aboard is the pilot.

On board, the jump key opens the launch sequence. Depending on the launcher, the capsule falls back, spends a few seconds weightless, or stays in orbit.

On the way back, arm the parachutes below 450 m (jump key): without them, the capsule crashes. If the launcher fails, the escape tower pulls the capsule away.

On the ground, sneak to get out; the capsule can be picked up. Three models: Mk1 (3 seats), Mk2 and Mk3 (4 seats).
guide.orbitalis.crewed_flight.title: Crewed Flight
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.scene.1: Place the electrolyzer against a water source, or empty a water bucket into it.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.scene.2: Hydrogen leaves on one side, oxygen on the other: place a liquefier on each side.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.scene.3: A tank against each liquefier collects the liquid propellant. Every machine must be powered.
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.text:
1. The electrolyzer splits water into hydrogen (left) and oxygen (right). Placed against water, it fills on its own.
2. A cryogenic liquefier on each side turns each gas into a liquid.

Gas pipes before the liquefiers, fluid pipes after. Every machine needs power.

The water pump, placed over at least 8 water blocks, gives one bucket per second forever.

If an output is full, the machine stops. The button under each output gauge sets its purge: 50%%, full, or off (right click).
guide.orbitalis.cryogenics.title: Oxygen and Hydrogen
guide.orbitalis.energy.scene.2: Open it and add fuel: coal, wood, a lava bucket...
guide.orbitalis.energy.scene.3: Place a machine against it: energy flows straight into it.
guide.orbitalis.energy.scene.4: A generator shares its energy between all the machines touching it.
guide.orbitalis.energy.text:
Machines run on electricity, counted in FE.

The combustion generator makes 20 FE per tick. Put fuel in the red slot (coal, wood, lava...), then place your machines against it or link them with cables. One coal gives 32,000 FE. When its buffer is full, it stops burning.

When broken, a machine keeps its energy and contents.
guide.orbitalis.energy.title: Energy
guide.orbitalis.engineering.text:
The engineer's workbench turns your technologies into hardware. To study a part, you need its technology and the materials for a prototype in your inventory. The study always succeeds, for the whole agency.

A studied part can be used on a rocket. A studied launcher can be printed ready-made at the design computer.

Green dot: done; blue: possible; orange: missing materials; grey: missing technology or parts.
guide.orbitalis.engineering.title: The Engineer's Workbench
guide.orbitalis.europa.text:
You need the Europa ship, an 18,500 m/s launcher with a nuclear stage, and an advanced suit with its radiation shielding module. Without it, you lose health outside.

Europa has no air: the ship lands on its engine, as on the Moon. Gravity is 13%%.

The cryobot melts through the ice down to the ocean in ten minutes. The first time, it finds signs of life there: the greatest discovery in the game.
guide.orbitalis.europa.title: Europa
guide.orbitalis.facilities.text:
The world hides space centers, far from villages and behind a fence: weather stations, research centers, observation centers and, more rarely, control centers with their launch pad. One in three is abandoned.

Their equipment no longer works: taken apart, it only gives scrap. Their chests hold plates, ingots, rocket parts, sometimes a satellite or a launch pad kit.

You often find an archive blueprint there, describing a ready-made rocket. Have it validated at the engineer's workbench, Archives tab.

The blocks of these buildings (concrete, cladding, tiles, glazing...) can be crafted too.
guide.orbitalis.facilities.title: Space Facilities
guide.orbitalis.fuels.scene.1: Place the refinery against a fuelled generator.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.scene.2: Put coal in the blue slot: each coal gives 250 mB of RP-1.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.scene.3: Place a tank against the refinery: it fills by itself.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.text:
A rocket engine burns propellants: a fuel and an oxidizer. To start with: RP-1 kerosene, liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen. Fluids are counted in mB (a bucket = 1,000 mB).

The refinery makes RP-1: one coal gives 250 mB in 5 seconds. Place a tank against it and it fills on its own.
guide.orbitalis.fuels.title: Fuels
guide.orbitalis.furnaces.text:
The induction furnace cooks with electricity everything a furnace cooks, twice as fast, for 20 FE per tick.

The melting furnace only takes ores and raw ores, but each one gives two ingots. It uses 60 FE per tick and needs the "Ore Refining" technology.
guide.orbitalis.furnaces.title: Electric Furnaces
guide.orbitalis.fusion.text:
The fusion engine ("Fusion Propulsion" technology) has 2,500 s of specific impulse and enough thrust for a crew. It burns liquid hydrogen and a little helium-3 (1 mB per 20 mB). It never ignites on the first stage.

At the launch pad, add a port set to helium-3.
guide.orbitalis.fusion.title: Fusion
guide.orbitalis.fusion_power.text:
The fusion reactor makes 1,200 FE per tick from helium-3 and hydrogen gas, brought in by pipe. It holds 1,000,000 FE in reserve.

The Casimir chamber turns an ender pearl into exotic matter, for 480,000 FE. One reactor powers three chambers.
guide.orbitalis.fusion_power.title: The Fusion Reactor
guide.orbitalis.helium3.text:
Helium-3, left by the solar wind in lunar regolith, is the ideal fuel for fusion. It needs the "Lunar Helium-3" technology.

The helium-3 extractor heats regolith (10 mB per block) or ilmenite ore (40 mB). Helium-3 comes out on the left, hydrogen on the right.
guide.orbitalis.helium3.title: Helium-3
guide.orbitalis.index.hint: Pick a chapter. Arrow: animated demo (drag to rotate, scroll to zoom).
guide.orbitalis.launch.text:
1. Build. Put the blueprint on the table of a working launch pad, then the blocks it shows.

2. Install. The rocket must fit under the tower and stay within the allowed mass. Sneak and right-click the table with an empty hand to take it back.

3. The sequence. It opens at the console, or on board with the jump key. One step per click, in order:
- Valves: fueling comes from the tanks connected to the ports. At 100%%, close them, or the pressure rises and the rocket explodes.
- Pressurization: without it, nothing ignites.
- Arm and walkway: retract them, or the rocket tears them off.
- Water deluge: without it, the flames break deck slabs.
- Ignition, then release the clamps at full thrust.

The poll ("Go / No-Go" window) checks that everything is ready before ignition. It is advised, not required.

4. The flight. The rocket follows its path on its own. You make the decisions shown in the middle of the screen before their gauge runs out: throttle down, separate each empty stage, jettison the fairing, cut the engines in orbit. A missed step fails the mission. Two or three times per flight, a gust asks you to hold or press a key in time.

The "Assist" button sets the flight computer: in assisted or automatic mode, it does some or all of the flight steps.

5. Afterwards. The agency gets its points: a bonus the first time it reaches a milestone, and data for every successful flight. The launcher is lost.

A rocket that explodes damages the pad around it, but the table and the deflector hold.

The atlas. The console's "Atlas" button opens the world map: launch pads, flights in progress, danger zones, clouds. Right-click to place a marker for the agency. With a communications satellite, the mission tablet opens the atlas anywhere.
guide.orbitalis.launch.title: Launch
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.1: Right-click with the kit, then pick the size and tower. Right-clicking the ground places the table, with the deflector below.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.10: Replace a frame block at the foot of the tower with a port, set by right-click. Link the console to a data port with a data cable.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.2: The flame deflector is buried under the table: the kit places it along with the table.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.3: The deck goes at table level, with an optional staircase on each side.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.4: The flame trench is a straight line of gratings from the table to the edge. The table turns them the right way by itself.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.5: A lightning mast stands on each corner, with a floodlight just below its top. The two deluge rails frame the rocket, open in the middle to leave room for the boosters.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.6: Start the tower with its utility column. It rises from the ground, against the deck, in the middle of the side facing the rocket.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.7: Then the rest of the tower, five blocks wide: the frame, the stairs and landings (or the elevator shaft), and a railed platform on top.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.8: The umbilical arm hangs from the utility column on the rocket side, and the boarding gate opens in the same face. The blueprint shows where they go.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.scene.9: With the last block in place, the blueprint disappears. Right-click the table to form the pad. If a block gets broken, the blueprint comes back to show what's missing.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.text:
A launch pad is built from a kit: a launch table, a flame deflector and paper. Right-click with the kit: pick the size and the tower (stairs or elevator). Right-clicking the ground places the table, with the deflector in place of the block below; a confirmation warns you first.

The plan shows up see-through. Place the blocks one by one, or right-click the table with an empty hand to place the whole yellow layer from what you carry.

The deck sits on the ground, with stairs on each side. These stairs are optional: remove them if you like.

With the last block, right-click the table to form the pad ("Launch Pad" technology). A broken block undoes it, and the plan comes back.

Ports: replace a frame block at the foot of the tower with a launch pad port. Right-click it with an empty hand to choose what it carries: a propellant, electricity or data. One port per propellant, with your tanks connected to it.

The pad uses electricity while it works: connect a cable to a deck slab, an energy port or the table.

The launch console links to a data port with a data cable, at any distance. Without a cable, you need a wireless module: right-click the console, then the pad.

Stay away at liftoff: the flames burn everything at the foot of the rocket.
guide.orbitalis.launch_complex.title: Launch Complex
guide.orbitalis.mars.text:
The Mars ship (8 t) needs a 13,000 m/s launcher.

In orbit, the sprint key prepares the departure, as for the Moon. The atmosphere slows the ship down, but you do the landing: hold the jump key to brake with the engine and follow the panel's advice. At touchdown: under 6 m/s down, 5 m/s sideways and 25° of tilt. In automatic mode, the computer lands for you.

On Mars, gravity is 38%%. To come back, hold the jump key for three seconds.

Farther out, probes explore Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Titan, Europa and Mercury.
guide.orbitalis.mars.title: Mars
guide.orbitalis.methane.text:
Methalox (liquid methane and oxygen) needs the "Methalox Engines" technology.

The Sabatier reactor makes methane from coal and hydrogen gas, and the liquefier turns it into a liquid. On Titan, the ice drill pumps the methane lakes directly.

At the launch pad, you need a port set to methane, as well as oxygen.
guide.orbitalis.methane.title: Methane
guide.orbitalis.missions.title: Which Pad for Which Mission
guide.orbitalis.moon.text:
You need a lunar ship (6 t), a 12,550 m/s launcher on a 9×9 pad, and a spacesuit.

In orbit, the sprint key prepares the departure. At the mark, hold it and release between 95 and 110%% of the delta-v. The ship lands on its own engine.

On the Moon, gravity is one sixth. The rock holds titanium, and some craters hold water ice. A sealed base with an air generator lets you breathe.

To come back, hold the jump key for three seconds on board.

Before a crew, you can send probes and robotic landers, launched like satellites.
guide.orbitalis.moon.title: The Moon
guide.orbitalis.ores.title: Ores
guide.orbitalis.overclocking.text:
Processing machines and fluid machines have a tab on the left of their screen. Put an overclock module in it: ×2, ×4 or ×8, each crafted from the previous one.

The module sets the top speed, and the button under it picks the speed: left click faster, right click slower. Going N times faster costs N² times the power: ×2 costs ×4, ×8 costs ×64.
guide.orbitalis.overclocking.title: Overclocking

guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.scene.4: The flame trench is a straight line of gratings from the table to the edge. The table turns them the right way by itself.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.scene.5: A lightning mast stands on each corner, with a floodlight just below its top. The two deluge rails frame the rocket, open in the middle to leave room for the boosters.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.scene.6: Start the tower with its utility column. It rises from the ground, against the deck, in the middle of the side facing the rocket.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.scene.7: Then the rest of the tower, five blocks wide: the frame, the stairs and landings (or the elevator shaft), and a railed platform on top.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.scene.8: The umbilical arm hangs from the utility column on the rocket side, and the boarding gate opens in the same face. The blueprint shows where they go.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.scene.9: With the last block in place, the blueprint disappears. Right-click the table to form the pad. If a block gets broken, the blueprint comes back to show what's missing.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.text:
The 11×11 launches up to 10,000 t and 44 blocks tall. Its tower has 46 levels, on 16×11 blocks of ground.

The demonstration builds it piece by piece. Scroll through it, turn it, zoom with the mouse wheel.
guide.orbitalis.pad_11x11.title: 11×11 Launch Pad

guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.scene.10: Replace a frame block at the foot of the tower with a port, set by right-click. Link the console to a data port with a data cable.

guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.scene.5: A lightning mast stands on each corner, with a floodlight just below its top. The two deluge rails frame the rocket, open in the middle to leave room for the boosters.
guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.scene.6: Start the tower with its utility column. It rises from the ground, against the deck, in the middle of the side facing the rocket.
guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.scene.7: Then the rest of the tower, five blocks wide: the frame, the stairs and landings (or the elevator shaft), and a railed platform on top.
guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.scene.8: The umbilical arm hangs from the utility column on the rocket side, and the boarding gate opens in the same face. The blueprint shows where they go.

guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.text:
The 9×9 launches up to 3,000 t and 36 blocks tall. Its tower has 38 levels, on 14×9 blocks of ground.

The demonstration builds it piece by piece. Scroll through it, turn it, zoom with the mouse wheel.
guide.orbitalis.pad_9x9.title: 9×9 Launch Pad
guide.orbitalis.pad_sizes.text:
Three sizes of launch pads with a tower, plus the test pad:
- 5×5: up to 200 t and 24 blocks tall, on 10×5 blocks. Probes, satellites, first crewed flights.
- 9×9: up to 3,000 t and 36 blocks, on 14×9. The Moon, Mars, high orbits.
- 11×11: up to 10,000 t and 44 blocks, on 16×11.

To change size, right-click the table with another kit. The kit gives the exact list of blocks.
guide.orbitalis.pad_sizes.title: The Three Launch Pads
guide.orbitalis.quarry.scene.1: Place the drill rig: it drills in front of it. The tower plan shows as a ghost.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.scene.2: Eight drill bases around it, on a 3×3 square.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.scene.3: A first full layer of nine drill masts.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.scene.4: A second layer: the 3×3×3 tower is complete and can drill.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.scene.5: Cable and water on any base block, and a chest against it for the loot.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.scene.6: Each extra layer widens and deepens the area, up to a 3×3×9 tower.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.text:
The drill rig digs the ground in front of it. Place it: the tower plan shows as a ghost. A 3×3 base (the drill rig in the middle of the front row, eight drill bases), then full layers of nine drill masts.

The taller the tower, the farther it drills: from 9×9 and 32 blocks deep (3 high) to 33×33 down to the bottom of the world (9 high).

Connect a cable and a water pipe to the base, put a chest against it, set the area and start. "Ores" only takes the ticked kinds; "Mine all" takes everything but fluids and containers.

The head heats up and water cools it. Core sampling reveals the ores under the area and gives research points.
guide.orbitalis.quarry.title: Drill Rig
guide.orbitalis.research.text:
The skill tree opens with the K key. A green box is learned, a blue one is available, a dark one waits for a prerequisite. Click a box to see its card, then "Research".

Points are earned by playing: goals reached and successful flights. Early on, launching sounding rockets is the fastest way.

In multiplayer, a team (/team) forms an agency that shares points and technologies.
guide.orbitalis.research.title: Research
guide.orbitalis.rocket_assembly.text:
The design computer draws the rocket: a model or a blank page, the payload, then up to three stages (engine, count, tanks). The first stage can carry two boosters. Delta-v, thrust and faults update live.

"Print blueprint" costs a sheet of paper and the payload. Right-click the table of a formed launch pad with the blueprint: the blocks to place appear layer by layer. Place them by hand, or from the build screen (right-click the table) with "Place layer" or "Place all".

The rocket forms with the last block. Sneak and right-click the table with an empty hand to take it apart.

Without a blueprint, stack an engine, tanks, then a bay and a nose cone above the table: it draws a blueprint by itself.
guide.orbitalis.rocket_assembly.title: Design and Build
guide.orbitalis.rocket_stats.text:
Mass: the full rocket. Thrust: the first stage. TWR (thrust / weight): it must be above 1, or the rocket does not lift off. Delta-v: the speed it can gain; to raise it, use a better engine, lighter tanks or one more stage.

Benchmarks: 1,700 m/s for space, 9,400 m/s for low orbit, 11,850 m/s for geostationary orbit.

Hydrogen is more efficient, but takes three times the room of RP-1.

The ion thruster and the solar sail only work in orbit. The nuclear thermal engine is for upper stages only.
guide.orbitalis.rocket_stats.title: Statistics
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.scene.1: Place the rolling mill against a fuelled generator.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.scene.2: Put an ingot in the blue slot.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.scene.3: Five seconds later, a plate arrives in the orange slot.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.text: The rolling mill flattens an ingot into a plate in 5 seconds: steel, aluminum, titanium or aluminum-lithium. Plates make the structure and tanks of rockets.
guide.orbitalis.rolling_mill.title: Rolling Mill
guide.orbitalis.satellites.title: Satellites
guide.orbitalis.shipyard.text:
An interstellar ship is built in orbit, at the shipyard attached to the station ("Orbital Shipyard" technology).

From inside the station, right-click a wall with the shipyard module to open a control room and a 31-block cradle.

The console holds the ship's plan. Place its blocks by hand or with "Build section". Fit out each section, load the core with eight exotic matter, then run the check at the pilot station.
guide.orbitalis.shipyard.title: The Shipyard
guide.orbitalis.space.text:
In orbit, you float and swim where you look. Jump to go up, sneak to go down.

To leave the capsule, you need a full spacesuit, with ten minutes of oxygen. The advanced suit lasts a quarter of an hour and takes modules (right-click with the module). It recharges on board.

To come home, board again and press the jump key. At the mark, hold it and release between 95 and 110%% of the requested delta-v. The capsule lands under parachutes near its launch pad.
guide.orbitalis.space.title: Space
guide.orbitalis.stations.text:
A station starts with its core module, launched uncrewed. It deploys in orbit, straight above the launch pad.

A crewed orbital flight from the same site docks with it on its own. Sneak to go through the airlock. The terminal shows power, air, orbit, crew and cargo.

The air generator pressurizes the station while it is powered. Solar panels produce in orbit but nothing during eclipse: plan for batteries.

Each module (habitat, laboratory, greenhouse, logistics, cupola, airlock, power truss) is brought aboard and deployed by right-clicking a wall.
guide.orbitalis.stations.title: Space Stations
guide.orbitalis.storage.scene.1: The cryogenic tank stores 32,000 mB of a single fluid.
guide.orbitalis.storage.scene.2: When powered, it keeps liquid oxygen and hydrogen without loss.
guide.orbitalis.storage.scene.3: Without energy, these propellants slowly boil off. RP-1 is not affected.
guide.orbitalis.storage.text:
The cryogenic tank holds 32,000 mB of one fluid. Powered (10 FE per tick), it keeps cold propellants; without power, they boil off.

The modular tank builds up to 3×3 and 12 high. It takes any fluid, one at a time, but is not cooled.

A tank pushes nothing: empty it with a pipe set to pull. When broken, it keeps its contents.

A control screen against a tank, or linked by data cable, shows its level. Screens side by side make a wall.
guide.orbitalis.storage.title: Storage
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.scene.1: Pick 3×3 in the kit. Right-clicking the ground places the table, and the plan appears.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.scene.2: The flame deflector is buried under the table: the kit places it along with the table.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.scene.3: Eight deck slabs around the table.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.scene.4: The flame trench: a line of grating, from the table to the edge.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.scene.5: With the last block, right-click the table to form the pad.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.scene.6: Power a deck slab, then link the test console to a data port with a data cable.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.text:
For your first sounding rockets, the test pad is enough: pick 3×3 in the kit. No tower, no masts.

It only takes uncrewed solid rockets, up to 20 t and 8 blocks tall.

Link the test console to a data port with a data cable, or with a wireless module. Open it and follow the list: ignition, then release the clamps at 100%% thrust.
guide.orbitalis.test_pad.title: The Test Pad
guide.orbitalis.titan.text:
The Titan ship (7 t) needs 17,500 m/s: you need a nuclear thermal stage.

On arrival, Titan's thick air slows the ship down, and its parachutes land it: arm them as when coming home.

It is -179 °C and the air is not breathable. Gravity is 14%%. Low ground is filled with liquid methane, which a bucket can scoop.

The flying drone studies the sites around and gives research points.
guide.orbitalis.titan.title: Titan
guide.orbitalis.title: Orbitalis Manual
guide.orbitalis.tracking_station.text:
The tracking station, placed under open sky, shows your satellites. "Receive data" turns their data into research points; a satellite holds three days of data at most. With a communications satellite, it arrives on its own.

The "Survey" tab shows the underground as seen by observation satellites.

The "Observatory" points your satellites at a body, visible only at certain times. Each discovery gives points, opens new ones and fills the catalog, which tells how to get there.
guide.orbitalis.tracking_station.title: The Tracking Station
guide.orbitalis.welcome.text:
Welcome to Orbitalis! This manual follows the progression, from the first ores up to rockets. Read the chapters in order.

First goal: steel. You need ores, energy and an arc foundry.

Almost everything is made from components, parts that only serve for crafting. The first ones are the heating element and the electric motor. Their tooltip says what they are for, and JEI shows their recipe.
guide.orbitalis.welcome.title: Welcome
item.orbitalis.battery_cell.desc: A lithium cell that stores electricity.
item.orbitalis.circuit_board.desc: The logic of machines, terminals and satellites.
item.orbitalis.co2_filter.desc: It removes carbon dioxide from the air you breathe.
item.orbitalis.display_screen.desc: The screens of consoles, terminals and tablets.
item.orbitalis.electric_motor.desc: It drives doors, mills and compressors.
item.orbitalis.flight_processor.desc: The brain of computers and launch pad automation.
item.orbitalis.heat_shield_tile.desc: It shields against flames and atmospheric re-entry.
item.orbitalis.heating_element.desc: The heart of furnaces and generators.
item.orbitalis.insulation_blanket.desc: Layers of gold foil: they keep the heat in, or the cold.
item.orbitalis.led_lamp.desc: A bright light that stays cool.
item.orbitalis.navigation_unit.desc: Gyroscopes and a clock: it always knows where you are.
item.orbitalis.optical_sensor.desc: The eye of telescopes and observation satellites.
item.orbitalis.overclock_module.hint: Goes in the left tab of a processing machine
item.orbitalis.radio_transmitter.desc: It links satellites to the ground.
item.orbitalis.reactor_core.desc: Fuel rods and their control: the heart of a nuclear engine.
item.orbitalis.reinforced_glass.desc: Portholes, visors and windows that hold pressure.
item.orbitalis.rocket_blueprint.unvalida: Unvalidated archived blueprint: have it studied at the engineer workbench, Archives tab.
item.orbitalis.steel_grating.desc: The grilles and walkways of towers and trenches.
key.orbitalis.moon: Leave for the Moon, hold (unbound: Sprint)
launch.orbitalis.burnout: Burnout: engines off, the rocket coasts upward.
launch.orbitalis.console.go_window.hint: Click a station to keep its explanation · Esc to close
launch.orbitalis.console.no_go: No go: fix the red lights
launch.orbitalis.event.orbit: Engine cutoff: in orbit at %s km. Margin: %s kg of propellant.
launch.orbitalis.event.space: Kármán line crossed: the rocket is in space.
launch.orbitalis.log.poll: Go / No-Go poll: all stations are GO
launch.orbitalis.mission_failed: Mission failed: a flight step was missed. No research points.
launch.orbitalis.power_lost: Power failure at the pad: valves closed, countdown scrubbed.
launch.orbitalis.scrubbed_weather: Launch scrubbed: bad weather over the pad.
launch.orbitalis.station.booster.desc: There must be a rocket on the table, no heavier than this pad can hold.
launch.orbitalis.station.flight.desc: The flight director gives the GO once every relevant station is green.
launch.orbitalis.station.ground.desc: The tower must be authorized, tall enough for this rocket, and carry at least one umbilical arm.
launch.orbitalis.station.guidance.desc: The flight computer needs a rocket assembled on the table to work out its trajectory.
launch.orbitalis.station.na_desc: This station does not apply to this rocket.

launch.orbitalis.station.range.desc: Stay at a safe distance from the launch table, and keep the sky clear above the rocket.
launch.orbitalis.station.weather.desc: No rain or storm over the pad. A weather satellite forecasts the next window.
launch.orbitalis.witness_points: Your agency earns %s research points for this launch.
observatory.orbitalis.body.andromeda.des: The great neighbour of our Galaxy: a trillion stars, 2.5 million light-years away. It is heading towards us, and the two galaxies will merge in four billion years.
observatory.orbitalis.body.comet.desc: A ball of ice and dust that returns every seventy years. Near the Sun it unfurls two tails: dust, curved and golden, and ions, straight and blue.
observatory.orbitalis.body.crab_pulsar.d: The remains of a star that exploded in 1054, recorded by Chinese astronomers. At its centre a neutron star spins thirty times a second, sweeping space with its beams.
Columns of gas and dust several light-years tall, in the Eagle Nebula. Stars are born at their tips, which the light of their neighbours slowly erodes.
observatory.orbitalis.body.europa.desc: A moon of Jupiter covered in ice, streaked with brown cracks. Beneath the ice lies an ocean of liquid water: one of the most promising places to look for life.
observatory.orbitalis.body.jupiter.desc: The giant of the solar system, with no surface, striped with cloud bands. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries.
observatory.orbitalis.body.kepler_452b.d: A super-Earth around a star like the Sun, a little older: it is called Earth's cousin. One and a half times as heavy, it could be covered in seas and plains.
observatory.orbitalis.body.large_magella: A small galaxy orbiting ours, 160,000 light-years away: a bar of stars, scattered clusters, and the Tarantula, the biggest star nursery known around us.
observatory.orbitalis.body.mars.desc: The red planet: iron-oxide deserts, giant volcanoes, ice caps. Its air, a hundred times thinner than ours, barely slows a spacecraft: a Mars lander touches down on its engine.
observatory.orbitalis.body.mercury.desc: The closest planet to the Sun, riddled with craters. Scorching by day, frozen by night; landing there takes more energy than reaching Pluto.
observatory.orbitalis.body.moon.desc: Our neighbour, three days away. Its dark basalt seas and craters keep the memory of the young solar system. A lunar module can land there.
A stellar nursery, 1,350 light-years away. At its heart four very young stars, the Trapezium, make all the gas glow: hydrogen in red, oxygen in teal.
observatory.orbitalis.body.pleiades.desc: A cluster of young blue stars, 440 light-years away, drifting through a dust cloud: their light reflects off it as a bluish veil.
observatory.orbitalis.body.proxima_b.des: The closest planet beyond the solar system, around a red dwarf. It lies where water could stay liquid, but its star's flares batter it relentlessly.
observatory.orbitalis.body.sagittarius_a: The black hole at the centre of our Galaxy, four million times the mass of the Sun. Nothing escapes it, not even light; around it, infalling gas glows, its light bent into a ring.
observatory.orbitalis.body.saturn.desc: The ringed planet: billions of blocks of ice, from grains to houses, in a sheet only a few tens of metres thick.
observatory.orbitalis.body.titan.desc: Saturn's great moon, under an orange haze thicker than our air. Methane rains down there, filling lakes and rivers. A parachute would almost be enough to land.
observatory.orbitalis.body.trappist_1e.d: One of seven Earth-sized planets circling a small, cool star. This one could hold oceans: a world to reach one day, at the end of a very long journey.
observatory.orbitalis.body.triangulum.de: The third galaxy of our group, after ours and Andromeda: a loose spiral with fluffy arms, dotted with pink clouds where stars are born.
observatory.orbitalis.body.venus.desc: Earth's twin in size, and a hell: clouds of acid, 92 bar of pressure and 465 °C at the surface. No probe has lasted more than two hours there.
observatory.orbitalis.body.whirlpool.des: A large spiral seen face-on, 23 million light-years away, with one arm touching a small companion galaxy: their meeting lights up stars all along the arms.
observatory.orbitalis.catalogue_empty: The catalogue is empty. Point your satellites at an object, then receive its image: it will appear here, with its card.

observatory.orbitalis.say.hidden: Out of sight for now: it comes back in %s.
observatory.orbitalis.say.imaged_hidden: In the catalogue. Visible again in %s.

observatory.orbitalis.say.observing: Observing, %s to go. Visible for %s more.
observatory.orbitalis.say.paused: Observation paused, out of sight: it comes back in %s.

recovery.orbitalis.plan: Rocket blueprint cancelled and returned. Blocks already placed stay where they are.

research.orbitalis.node.aluminum_lithium: Lighter and stiffer: every kilogram saved adds delta-v.
research.orbitalis.node.aluminum_structu: Light tanks and hulls made of aluminum plates.
research.orbitalis.node.capsules.desc: First crewed flights, like Vostok and Mercury.
research.orbitalis.node.closed_loop_life: Air and water recycling for long stays.
research.orbitalis.node.communication_sa: Long-range communication and relays for probes.
research.orbitalis.node.cryobot.desc: A probe that melts the ice to go down to a hidden ocean. Unlocks the cryobot, to look for life under Europa's ice.
research.orbitalis.node.europa_lander.de: Land on Europa, under Jupiter's radiation, and leave again. Also unlocks the suit's radiation shielding.
A sphere and a radio transmitter: the space age begins, as with Sputnik.
research.orbitalis.node.flight_computers: Automatic guidance, from ignition to orbit insertion.
research.orbitalis.node.fuel_cells.desc: Electricity and water from hydrogen and oxygen, as on Gemini and Apollo. Essential for long missions: it opens orbital rendezvous.
research.orbitalis.node.fuel_farm.desc: Propellant storage and lines to the launch pad. Lets you place fuel ports.
research.orbitalis.node.fusion.desc: The power of stars, to cross the solar system. Unlocks the fusion drive, which burns helium-3 from the Moon, and the fusion reactor, which turns it into electricity.
research.orbitalis.node.gyroscopes.desc: They measure the rocket's attitude and keep it on course.
research.orbitalis.node.heat_shields.des: Tiles and ablative shields to survive atmospheric reentry.
research.orbitalis.node.helium3.desc: Bake the Moon's regolith to free the solar wind's helium-3, the fuel of fusion. Unlocks the helium-3 extractor.
research.orbitalis.node.hydrolox_engines: The best chemical efficiency, like Vulcain or RS-25. Ideal for upper stages.
research.orbitalis.node.hypergolics.desc: Hydrazine and its relatives ignite on contact. Unlocks the hypergolic engine, loaded at the factory: no fuelling at the pad.
research.orbitalis.node.ion_propulsion.d: Tiny thrust but huge efficiency, using xenon. Unlocks the ion thruster, an upper stage for probes and satellites: once in orbit, it adds thousands of m/s of delta-v.
research.orbitalis.node.isru.desc: Make water, oxygen and fuel from local resources. Unlocks the ice drill (Moon, Mars) and the oxygen extractor (Mars).
Turbopump engines burning kerosene and liquid oxygen, like Merlin, F-1 or RD-180.
research.orbitalis.node.landers.desc: Land softly on another celestial body. Unlocks the robotic landers, which really touch down on the Moon or Mars.
research.orbitalis.node.launch_escape.de: A tower pulls the capsule away from a failing rocket. Without it, the crew is hurt when their rocket breaks up.
research.orbitalis.node.launch_pad.desc: Launch table and flame trench for the first rockets.
research.orbitalis.node.life_support.des: Oxygen, pressure and temperature: what it takes to keep a crew alive.
research.orbitalis.node.lunar_gateway.de: An outpost around the Moon, like the Lunar Gateway. Unlocks the lunar gateway, launched like a satellite, which earns points every day from lunar orbit.
research.orbitalis.node.lunar_lander.des: Land on the Moon and take off again, like the Apollo lunar module.
research.orbitalis.node.mars_lander.desc: Land on Mars by hand, on its engine, and leave again.
research.orbitalis.node.methalox_engines: Reusable full-flow engines, like Raptor or BE-4. Unlocks the methalox engine and the Sabatier reactor, which makes methane from coal and hydrogen.
Telemetry screens and trajectory tracking during the mission. Lets you place mission displays.
research.orbitalis.node.mission_tablet.d: The atlas in your hand, wherever a communication satellite relays the data.
research.orbitalis.node.navigation_satel: A medium-orbit constellation gives your position anywhere.
A reactor heats hydrogen, like NERVA. Unlocks the nuclear thermal engine, twice as efficient as a chemical engine but heavy and hungry for tanks. It's only for upper stages. Also unlocks the hydrogen tank, big and light, made for it.
research.orbitalis.node.orbital_shipyard: Building in orbit what no rocket could ever launch: a ship for other stars. Unlocks the shipyard module.
research.orbitalis.node.ore_refining.des: The melting furnace, which gets twice as many ingots out of every ore.
Habitats, power plants and greenhouses for a lasting presence. Unlocks the planetary base kit, which builds a pressurised module on the Moon or Mars.
research.orbitalis.node.pressure_fed_eng: First liquid engines, fed by tank pressure.
research.orbitalis.node.probes.desc: They fly past other worlds and send data back. Unlocks the lunar and Mars probes, which map the body from orbit.
research.orbitalis.node.rendezvous_docki: Two spacecraft meet in orbit, as in the Gemini program.
research.orbitalis.node.robotic_arm.desc: It grabs cargo as it arrives, like Canadarm2: what a launcher delivers to the station is stowed in a cargo rack.
research.orbitalis.node.rotorcraft.desc: Rotor drones, like Ingenuity on Mars and Dragonfly on Titan. Unlocks the rotor drone, which flies off alone to study nearby sites.
research.orbitalis.node.rovers.desc: Exploration vehicles, like the LRV, Curiosity or Perseverance. Unlocks the rover, a solar-powered lunar buggy you set down and drive.
research.orbitalis.node.rtg.desc: A power source for decades, far from the Sun: satellites launched afterwards last twice as long.
research.orbitalis.node.sample_return.de: Bring rocks back to Earth for research. Unlocks robotic sample return missions and the sample container, to take samples yourself.
research.orbitalis.node.service_tower.de: Umbilical arms, access to the rocket and hold-down clamps.
research.orbitalis.node.solar_arrays.des: Truss, Sun-tracking solar arrays and radiators.
research.orbitalis.node.solar_power.desc: Electrical power in orbit, as long as the Sun is in view. Lets you place solar panels.
research.orbitalis.node.solar_sails.desc: Sunlight pushes a huge sail, with no fuel. Unlocks the solar sail, an upper stage with no propellant, all the better as the payload is light.
research.orbitalis.node.solid_boosters.d: Large strap-on boosters, as on Ariane 5 or the Space Shuttle. Unlocks the solid booster.
research.orbitalis.node.solid_motors.des: Solid propellant: simple and reliable, but it cannot be shut down. The engine of sounding rockets.
research.orbitalis.node.sounding_payload: Instruments that measure the upper atmosphere during a suborbital flight.
research.orbitalis.node.space_telescopes: They discover new worlds and unlock destinations.
research.orbitalis.node.spacesuits.desc: Suits for launch and for spacewalks.
research.orbitalis.node.staged_combustio: All propellant goes through the main chamber: more thrust and efficiency.
Cheap and strong at both very low and very high temperatures, as on Starship. Unlocks the large stainless tank.
Habitation modules, laboratories and connecting nodes.
research.orbitalis.node.steelmaking.desc: Steel, made in the arc foundry. Known from the start.
research.orbitalis.node.superalloys.desc: Inconel-type alloys that withstand combustion chamber heat. Unlocks the vacuum engine, for upper stages.
research.orbitalis.node.telemetry.desc: The rocket sends its measurements to the ground during flight: every flight that reaches space earns 3 more points.
research.orbitalis.node.test_stands.desc: Engine tests earn research points: each engine studied at the engineer workbench gives 15.
research.orbitalis.node.titan_lander.des: Land on Titan under parachutes, like the Huygens probe, and leave again.
research.orbitalis.node.titanium_parts.d: Strong and light, for the most heavily loaded parts. Unlocks the titanium tank, the lightest.
research.orbitalis.node.tracking_station: Large antennas to stay in touch with distant spacecraft. Opens the tracking station's observatory and survey.
research.orbitalis.node.vehicle_assembly: Large launchers are assembled indoors, then rolled out to the pad. Allows three-stage launchers.
research.orbitalis.node.warp_drive.desc: Folding space to reach other stars. Unlocks the warp core, charged with exotic matter, which the Casimir chamber draws from the vacuum.

sequence.orbitalis.not_ready: The pad or the rocket is not ready: see the control centre board.
sequence.orbitalis.overpressure.burst: Overpressure: the tanks gave way. The rocket exploded on its pad.

sequence.orbitalis.poll.missing: No go/no-go poll: ignition at your own risk.
sequence.orbitalis.poll.no_go: Poll: a station is no-go. No ignition.
sequence.orbitalis.poll.refused: A station said no-go. Fix it, then run the poll again.
sequence.orbitalis.pressure_lost: Tank pressure has dropped: part of the cold propellants went with it.
sequence.orbitalis.scorched: Without the deluge, the flames broke the deck. Slabs lost: %s.
sequence.orbitalis.step.chill.desc: Chills the turbopump engines with cryogenic propellant. The chill-down only holds for two minutes.
sequence.orbitalis.step.cutoff.desc: Shuts the engines down at the right speed: too early or too late and the orbit is missed.
sequence.orbitalis.step.deluge.desc: Floods the base of the pad to soak up the noise and heat of liftoff.
sequence.orbitalis.step.fairing.desc: Jettisons the fairing once out of the atmosphere: the payload no longer needs it.
sequence.orbitalis.step.ignite.desc: Lights the engines. Thrust builds over three seconds while the clamps hold the rocket down.
sequence.orbitalis.step.internal.desc: Switches the rocket to its own batteries: it leaves ground power before liftoff.
sequence.orbitalis.step.poll.desc: Asks every mission control station before ignition, to find out what isn't ready.
sequence.orbitalis.step.pressurize.desc: Pressurizes the tanks to feed the engines. It only holds for two minutes, so ignite before then.
sequence.orbitalis.step.release.desc: Releases the clamps once thrust reaches 100%: liftoff.
sequence.orbitalis.step.retract.desc: Swings the umbilical arm and the gangway away from the rocket. Do it before ignition.
sequence.orbitalis.step.stage.desc: Drops the empty stage and lights the next one, inside the shown window.
sequence.orbitalis.step.test_alarm.desc: Sounds the pad alarm: sirens and beacons.
sequence.orbitalis.step.test_arms.desc: Swings the tower arms to check that they clear the rocket.
sequence.orbitalis.step.test_deluge.desc: Opens the deluge to watch the water flow, with no rocket and no countdown.
sequence.orbitalis.step.throttle.desc: Throttles down through max-Q to spare the structure.
sequence.orbitalis.step.valves.desc: Opens the valves to fuel up from the pad. Close them at 100%, or the pressure climbs too high.
sequence.orbitalis.test.arm_away: The arm is already retracted: put it back before the test.
sequence.orbitalis.test.no_pad: The launch pad is not in service: no test possible.
sequence.orbitalis.test.valves: Close the valves before swinging the arm away.
